# Web front ends: where to start

How UI state is shaped and owned, how big components get before they are split, and what the client may be trusted with and tested for.

Flags: **C** contested (offer it as a choice, with both sides) · **A** agents do this readily · **T** has a one-file tell · **E** has a pseudo-code example.

Axes in brackets: ⊕ the lens's primary effect, the reason to reach for it · + also helps · − costs. Laws name the axes they bear on. See [AXES.md](../AXES.md).

`{kinds}`: where it matters most. `langs:` which languages have notes. `→` related lenses.

## Probes for the interview

Find first, in the code, docs, git history, CI and config. Ask only what the repository can't tell, in the project's own terms, with the evidence and a recommendation. Skip the question when the findings settle it. Also see the general stances in [THINKING.md](../THINKING.md).

### 1. High Test Maintenance Cost

**Find:** Test files changed in commits that only restyled or restructured components. Whether those tests query by markup, class names or snapshots, or by role, label and visible text. Which style recent tests use.

**Ask:** "Restyling commits <commits> also changed <N> tests, mostly <snapshot / class-selector> ones. I'd have new tests query by role and visible text, because they then survive a restyle. Agree, or do the snapshots earn their keep for you?"

**Settled when:** Tests already query by behaviour and restyling commits rarely touch them. The agent confirms that as the rule.

### 2. The Hype Cycle & Amara's Law

**Find:** When each dependency was added (package manifest and lockfile history). For the recent ones: how many usage styles coexist (old and new APIs, two state or data-fetching libraries side by side), the direction over time, and any migration notes.

**Ask:** "<lib> came in <when> and is used <N> different ways across <files>, while <older lib> still covers <M>. New code since <date> uses <style>. Is it settled? I'd write conventions around <style> <now / once X> because <reason>."

**Settled when:** One idiom is used throughout and the older library is gone. The agent confirms it and moves on.

### 3. Not Invented Here, Emotional Attachment

**Find:** In-house components, hooks and state helpers that do what the framework or a dependency already in the manifest provides. Size, how many call sites, last change, authors, and any comment or commit saying why they exist.

**Ask:** "<helper> does what <framework feature / library> does, <differing only in X>. Keep it as the house way, or move new code to <x>? I'd <recommend> because <reason>; if you'd keep it, I'll record why."

**Settled when:** A comment or doc gives a reason that still holds. The agent cites it and asks only whether new code should use it.

### 4. Defense in depth

**Find:** Decisions the client makes: permission checks that hide or disable UI, price or quantity calculations, form validation. For each, whether the endpoint it calls checks the same thing (when the server code is in reach). List what is checked only in the client.

**Ask:** "<checks> happen only in the client (<files>); the server <does / doesn't> repeat them for <endpoints>. I'd require the server to check <x> regardless of the UI, because <anyone can call the API directly>. Is there anything the client may decide on its own?"

**Settled when:** Every client-side check has a server equivalent. When the server code isn't in reach, this is always an ask.
